title: British butterfly communities followed about 14% of their spatial temperature gradient in 1976-2024 with European niche indices; GB-internal indices gave 62% because they carry non-climatic losses
abstract: Question: campaign work found that community temperature indices (CTI) follow only a small part of their spatial temperature gradient in time (birds below 10-24%, 75 networks about 12%), while British butterflies seemed to follow about half. Which processes set the gap? Data (outside BBS): UK Butterfly Monitoring Scheme site indices 1976-2024 (686 GB sites with 10 or more well-monitored years, 12,900 site-years, 55 taxa), E-OBS v32.0e temperature, GBIF density maps (1990-2024), BNM distribution trends. Method: CTI split exactly into an incidence channel and a relative-abundance channel; spatial slope of site CTI on climatology; slow (site warming trend) and fast (anomaly) temporal slopes with site effects; joint bootstrap over 50 km blocks and 5-year year blocks; split of long-site change into taxa gained, lost and persistent against a permutation null; within-species occupancy and abundance transfer. Post hoc: species temperature indices (STI) from European GBIF distributions in place of the usual STI from the network's own sites. Results: with GB-internal STIs the slow fraction was 0.62 (95% CI 0.38-1.17), all through incidence. Within species, occupancy followed 0.10 (SE 0.03) and abundance 0.01 (0.05) of the gradient, so national gains and losses of whole taxa drove the CTI. GB and European STIs correlated at only 0.53. The part of the GB STI not predicted by the European STI was linked to decline (Spearman 0.40 with UKBMS occupancy trends, 0.28 with independent atlas trends) and carried 82% of the slow trend. With European STIs the slow fraction was 0.14 (-0.27 to 0.39); 0.06-0.20 in three variants. Gains of warm-niche taxa gave 0.19 (0.06-0.32) of the expected change, but losses of warm-niche taxa (Wall, Duke of Burgundy, Grayling) went against it (-0.08). Conclusion: butterflies are not an exception; slow colonisation plus non-climatic losses set the gap, and STIs taken from a network's own sites can make non-climatic declines look like climate tracking. Limitations: the European STI test is post hoc; GBIF effort bias; national trends confound slow slopes; wide intervals.

display.caption: Site-centred CTI of 686 UKBMS sites by year (dots: year means; line: 5-year mean) with the full space-for-time expectation (dashed) and the fitted slow response (dotted). Left: GB-internal cross-fitted STI (slow fraction 0.62). Right: European STI from GBIF and E-OBS (0.14).

Slow fraction (temporal / spatial slope) by STI source and channel (all, incidence, relative abundance), and the spatial and slow temporal slopes; 95% joint block bootstrap intervals. The GB mean STI equals its European-predicted part plus its residual; the residual carries most of the slow trend.

Left: GB-internal against European STI of 52 taxa, coloured by the BNM long-term GB distribution trend. Right: GB STI residual from the European fit against the UKBMS occupancy trend. Taxa that sit colder in GB than their European niche predicts declined.
